newsitem.title: USA: Alumina prices to remain strong medium-term - CRU.
newsitem.headline: Alumina prices to remain strong medium-term - CRU.

text.p: Alumina prices will remain strong in the medium term, riding on the back of firm aluminum prices as demand grows, Mark Fraser of consultancy CRU International said.
Fraser expected a moderate alumina market deficit this year and idled refinery capacity will have to come on stream soon to avoid tightness.
Prices for alumina were expected to remain about $200 a tonne, Fraser told Metal Bulletin's Bauxite and Alumina Seminar.
Chinese alumina imports should be stronger this year, totaling about 1.4 million tonnes with the bulk of this yet to be shipped.
But further alumina price hikes were likely to be moderated by restarts of aluminum capacity, but large price falls were ruled out, Fraser said.
"We do not expect further restarts of aluminium capacity this year after Norsk Hydro AS. Players will wait to see how existing restarts are absorbed in the market," Fraser said.
He did not expect aluminum restarts - the bulk of idled capacity is held by Aluminum Co of America, Alcan Aluminum Ltd and Reynolds Metals Co - until 1999 because of current high LME aluminum stocks.
Western alumina demand will rise by a total of 2.37 million tonnes between 1998 and 2001 while Chinese imports were expected to remain at about 1.4 million a year in this period.
"CIS buying amounts to 2 million tonnes a year and this is expected to remain stable until 2001," Fraser said.
Any CIS alumina refinery that was going to close would have done so by now. "Aluminium prices will be strong enough to allow continued operation of CIS plants," Fraser said.

CRU forecast that Western world primary aluminum consumption will grow 4.7 percent to 18.3 million tonnes this year. In 1998 to 2001 consumption will grow 2.4 percent a year to 20 milion tonnes by the end of the century.
Such a growth forecast will mean that another 4 million tonnes of alumina will be needed by 2001. Alumina output will have to rise 1,000,000 tonnes in 1998 and a similar hike each year thereafter.
"The market will look to the West to fill the gap even though Eastern Bloc (alumina) refineries are below capacity," Fraser said.
After Western refineries have cranked up their output, 2.5 million tonnes of new alumina capacity will be needed from 1999, CRU estimated.
Much of the new brownfield and greenfield capacity will be in Australia.

The likely brownfield expansions were 900,000 tonnes at Worsley, 850,000 tonnes at Wagerup, 300,000 tonnes at Gove. Likely greenfield projects were 1 million tonnes at Weipa, and 1 million tonnes at Uktal in India, Fraser said.
